extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, regulated utilities and industry stakeholders, environmental NGOs, and legal practitioners commenting on/implementing CAA section 111 rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the EPA (and states implementing EPA emission guidelines) must identify the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER), determine the degree of emission limitation achievable, and (where appropriate) create subcategories and compliance timeframes under CAA section 111 for new and existing sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to the Source Category and Subcategorizing
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111 requires EPA to list stationary source categories that may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare and authorizes EPA discretion whether to "distinguish among classes, types, and sizes within categories of new sources for the purpose of establishing [new source] standards," i.e., to subcategorize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has long interpreted section 111(d) to authorize subcategorization for existing sources as well. The Administrator is entitled to a "high degree of deference" on subcategorization because it entails scientific judgment. The EPA's 1975 implementing regulation provides the Administrator will specify different emission guidelines or compliance times for different sizes, types, and classes when based on costs of control, physical limitations, geographical location, or similar factors. Examples of bases used historically include size (heat input capacity), type of fuel combusted, equipment types, manufacturing processes, levels of utilization, activity level (active/closed landfills), and geographic location.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of Emission Reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: A "system of emission reduction" is the set of measures the EPA identifies as the basis for a standard of performance; while the CAA does not define the phrase, it at minimum includes measures that an individual source applies that improve the emissions performance of that source and may include off-site activities (e.g., precombustion cleaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically EPA has selected systems like efficiency improvements, fuel-switching, and add-on controls. The Supreme Court in West Virginia recognized that such traditional measures fall comfortably within prior practice. The EPA should identify concrete measures that reduce an individual source's contribution to pollution.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Adequately Demonstrated" requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111(a)(1) the Administrator must determine that a candidate system of emission reduction "has been adequately demonstrated"; this is an essential (though not sufficient) condition for using a system as the basis for an achievable emission standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term does not require the system to be in widespread commercial use at rule publication; EPA may rely on demonstration projects, pilot tests, or examples of technological feasibility. Legislative history and caselaw support EPA's authority to adopt technology-forcing measures that are not yet widespread, provided sufficient evidence exists to extrapolate feasibility (see Ruckelshaus, Sierra Club v. Costle, Lignite Energy Council).

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievability of the standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of performance must reflect a "degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the [BSER]"—i.e., the standard must be achievable through application of the chosen system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achievability means the EPA's record-based finding that affected sources can adopt the specific system to achieve the specified degree of limitation. EPA may set standards more stringent than historically achieved based on identified technological improvements and may extrapolate from pilot/commercial data to support achievability (Essex Chem. Corp. v. Ruckelshaus; Sierra Club v. Costle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory factors to consider when selecting BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining BSER and the degree of emission limitation, EPA must take into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any non-air quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caselaw additionally identifies consideration of the amount of air pollution reduced and the role of technological innovation. The EPA may weigh these factors against each other and has discretion in doing so; its approach should evaluate the amount of emission reductions, costs, non-air impacts, and energy requirements when choosing the "best" system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extrapolation and qualitative methods (compensating for limited data)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may reasonably extrapolate from available data (pilot projects, test sources, performance in other industries) and may use qualitative methods to compensate for shortages of data when determining that a technology is "adequately demonstrated" or that a standard is achievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrapolation is permissible where supported by evidence; however, EPA may not base determinations on mere speculation or conjecture. The Lignite decision permits reasonable extrapolation but cautions against speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible evidence types for an "adequately demonstrated" finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence supporting an "adequately demonstrated" determination may include test sources, individual commercial-scale sources, demonstration projects/plants, pilot tests, studies, and performance data from other jurisdictions or related industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Ruckelshaus upheld extrapolation from a lone U.S. plant (and broader European experience); Lignite upheld extrapolation from related-source data; EPA may rely on demonstration plant results and other experiments or studies to show technological feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance timeframe / deployment at scale
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must demonstrate that the industry can deploy the chosen system of emission reduction at scale within the compliance timeframe set by the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a system is adequately demonstrated, EPA must show that sources can reasonably adopt it in the time allowed; compliance-time considerations are part of assessing achievability and may affect the degree of emission limitation set.

rubrics_metrics.name: States' flexibility in implementing emission guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: For CAA section 111(d) emission guidelines, EPA determines the BSER and degree of emission limitation, but states have flexibility in how they assign standards of performance to affected sources and in choosing compliance mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may ensure that the standards they establish represent the equivalent of EPA's performance rates and may employ trading, averaging, or other programs in their state plans; EPA's preamble notes that neither states nor sources are required to apply the specific measures identified in the BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategorization bases / relevant characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: When subcategorizing a source category, EPA may consider characteristics that make different emission controls more appropriate for different sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible bases (illustrated by historical rulemakings) include size (e.g., heat input capacity), type of fuel combusted, type of equipment, manufacturing process, levels of utilization, activity level, and geographic location. The 1975 implementing regulation lists costs of control, physical limitations, geographical location, or similar factors as grounds for differing guidelines or compliance times.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER determination process (structured approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's approach: identify systems of emission reduction that have been adequately demonstrated; evaluate each candidate by the amount of emission reductions, costs, non-air health and environmental impacts, and energy requirements; determine which system is the "best"; then determine the achievable emission limit based on application of that BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For CAA section 111(b) EPA sets the standard of performance reflecting the achievable emission limit; under section 111(d) EPA sets the degree of emission limitation and states must establish standards of performance that reflect that degree. The EPA's determinations should be documented with supporting analysis of the statutory factors and relevant precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'standard of performance' (statutory text)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term "standard of performance" means a standard for emission of air pollutants which reflects the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the best system of emission reduction which (taking into account the cost of achieving such reduction and any non-air quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements) the Administrator determines has been adequately demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory text is the controlling definition for what the EPA must reflect in any standard; EPA's analyses should explicitly connect chosen BSER and degree of limitation to the statutory text and listed factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: cannot base determinations on mere speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where data are unavailable, EPA may not base its determination that a technology is adequately demonstrated or a standard is achievable on mere speculation or conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While EPA can use reasonable extrapolation and qualitative methods to address data gaps, the record must provide a non-speculative basis for the Agency's conclusions (per Lignite Energy Council and related caselaw).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine consideration for generation-shifting BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that a generation-shifting BSER (as in the Clean Power Plan) implicated the "major questions" doctrine and required clear congressional authorization because it would restructure the Nation's overall mix of electricity generation and represented a transformative expansion in regulatory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should recognize that measures constituting market- or system-wide restructuring (e.g., prescribing market shares of coal, gas, wind, solar) may be treated by courts as raising major questions and may require clear congressional authorization; by contrast, traditional measures improving individual-source performance (fuel-switching, add-on controls, efficiency improvements) have historically been treated as within EPA's section 111 practice.
